t: Find Kth Largest XOR Coordinate Value - 2D Prefix XOR Plus Selection
o: The value of coordinate (i, j) of an m x n matrix is the XOR of every entry in the rectangle from the origin down to (i, j) - a 2D prefix sum computed with XOR instead of addition - and among all m*n coordinate values we must return the k-th largest (1-indexed). For `matrix = [[5,2],[1,6]]` the four values are 5, 5^2 = 7, 5^1 = 4 and 5^2^1^6 = 0; sorted descending that is [7, 5, 4, 0], so k = 1, 2, 3 return 7, 5, 4 - exactly the three examples. With m and n up to 1000 there can be a million values, so recomputing each rectangle from scratch is hopeless; luckily XOR is self-inverse, so the same inclusion-exclusion trick used for prefix sums derives every value in O(1) from its three already-computed neighbors. Once all values exist the task is ordinary selection, and even a full sort of a million integers is comfortably fast.
k: XOR is associative, commutative and self-inverse, so 2D prefix XOR obeys the identical recurrence as 2D prefix sum: P[i][j] = M[i][j] ^ P[i-1][j] ^ P[i][j-1] ^ P[i-1][j-1].
A full (m+1) x (n+1) table is unnecessary: a rolling column array plus a running row accumulator produce each prefix value in place while scanning once.
After the mn values exist this is generic k-th-largest selection; keeping a size-k min-heap caps the selection cost at O(mn log k).

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix XOR + Sort All Values
a.i: Generate every coordinate value with the prefix-XOR recurrence while sweeping the matrix once, collect them in one array, sort descending and read off index k-1. Simple to reason about and fast in practice for mn up to one million.
s: Maintain col[j] = XOR of matrix[0..i][j] for the current row i, plus a running row accumulator.
For each cell: col[j] ^= matrix[i][j], then row ^= col[j]; row now equals the value of coordinate (i, j).
Append every value to a list.
Sort the list in descending order and return element k-1.
a.t: O(mn log(mn)) - computing prefixes is linear; sorting all mn values dominates.
a.sp: O(mn) - the list of all coordinate values (plus O(n) rolling state).

a.n: Approach 2: Stream Through a Size-k Min-Heap
a.i: We only need the k-th largest element, not a total order. Stream the values through a min-heap capped at size k: it always holds the k largest values seen so far and its root is the current k-th largest. An incoming value replaces the root only when strictly greater. Memory beyond the input drops from O(mn) to O(k), and time improves whenever k is much smaller than mn.
s: Compute values row by row exactly as in Approach 1.
While the heap holds fewer than k elements, push each value.
Otherwise replace the root when the incoming value is strictly larger than it.
At the end return the heap root.
a.t: O(mn log k) - each of the mn values costs at most one O(log k) heap operation.
a.sp: O(k) - the heap, plus O(n) rolling column state.

w: Lead with Approach 1 in an interview - it is short and provably correct - then offer the heap as the refinement when asked about space or small k. Pitfalls: do not reuse sum-style code and flip signs; write the XOR recurrence from scratch since inclusion-exclusion with XOR has no subtraction; remember k is 1-indexed into descending order; and prefer the rolling column array over allocating an (m+1)(n+1) table. Follow-ups: return all top-k values (the heap already contains them), support point updates to the matrix (needs a 2D BIT over XORs), or compute the value of an arbitrary subrectangle rather than origin-fixed ones.
